lessons.title: Expressions and factorising
lessons.summary: Translate situations into expressions, collect like terms, expand and factorise.
lessons.objective: Translate situations into expressions, collect like terms, expand and factorise.
lessons.before: A letter can name a changing quantity in an expression. A formula links quantities. An equation asks where two expressions are equal.
lessons.ideas:
Terms are like terms only if they have the same variable part, including the powers. Combine their coefficients and keep the variable part.

An expression records a calculation. Use a variable for a quantity that can change. Multiply the rate by the variable and add any fixed amount.

Multiply the outside factor by each inside term. Multiply coefficients and add exponents for matching bases.

Find the highest common factor of the coefficients and the lowest power of each shared letter. Divide every term by this factor to find what remains in the bracket.
lessons.method:
When substituting, put negative numbers in brackets before applying a power.

Check your expression with a value of zero or one.

Check whether the degree of each term makes sense.

Expand your answer to check that it matches the original.
mistakes: x and x² are different terms.
A one-off charge is not multiplied by the number of items.
Remember the sign of each term and multiply the last term too.
A term might contain x without containing x².

examples.title: Collecting terms with matching powers
examples.question:
A learner writes \(5x+3x^2-x\).

  1. Collect the terms and simplify.

    [2]

  2. Evaluate the expression when \(x=2\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The terms \(5x\) and \(-x\) use the same power of x. Combine their coefficients.

The squared term has a different power and stays separate.

\(3x^2+4x\)

(b) Substitute 2 for x. Square 2 before multiplying by the coefficient.

\(20\)

examples.title: Writing a club cost as an expression
examples.question:
A coding club charges 18 credits for entry and \(3\) credits for each activity. A learner tries n activities.

  1. Write an expression for the total charge.

    [2]

  2. Explain why \((18+3)n\) does not describe this cost.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The activities cost \(3\) credits each, so they cost \(3n\) altogether.

Add the one fixed entry charge of 18 credits.

\(18+3n\)

(b) A bracket multiplied by n means both charges repeat n times.

It would charge the entry fee for every activity.

examples.title: Expanding terms with powers
examples.question:
The expression is \(9x(4x^2-1)\).

  1. Expand the brackets.

    [2]

  2. Check your result when x = 1.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Apply the outside factor to both terms. The first multiplication combines \(x\) and \(x^2\) to make \(x^3\).

The second product keeps the minus sign.

\(36x^3-9x\)

(b) Set x to 1. Each positive power of 1 still equals 1.

\(27\)

examples.title: Finding the greatest common algebraic factor
examples.question:
Consider \(18x^2+21x\).

  1. What is the highest common factor of both terms?

    [2]

  2. Factorise the expression fully.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The integers 18 and 21 have highest common factor 3 because 6 and 7 are consecutive.

Both terms contain x, while only the first includes a second x factor.

\(3x\)

(b) Divide each term by the common factor to obtain the two terms inside the bracket. Multiply back to check.

\(3x(6x+7)\)

lessons.title: Equations, formulae and intervals
lessons.summary: Use inverse operations to solve equations, rearrange formulae and interpret interval boundaries.
lessons.objective: Use inverse operations to solve equations, rearrange formulae and interpret interval boundaries.
lessons.before: Read the equals sign as a balance. Both sides have the same value.
lessons.ideas:
Collect the variable terms on one side. Reverse the remaining operations one at a time. Do the same on both sides.

Undo any addition or subtraction outside the fraction. Then multiply by the denominator to undo the division.

To make a letter the subject, isolate it on one side. Use inverse operations on both sides even when the other side contains letters.

A strict inequality excludes its endpoint. A sign including equality includes its endpoint. On a number line use an open circle for excluded and a filled circle for included.
lessons.method:
Always check your solution in the original equation.

Record the operation on each line so a reader can follow.

Check a rearranged formula using a simple original value.

If the variable stands for a whole number, list only whole numbers inside the interval.
mistakes: Moving a term is shorthand for adding or subtracting on both sides.
Undo operations in reverse order. Multiplying first is valid only if every term is multiplied.
Rearranging a formula does not require numerical values.
Read the upper and lower signs individually.

examples.title: Two plans cost the same
examples.question:
Plan P costs \(5x+18\) credits. Plan Q costs \(7x+4\) credits. The number of uses is x.

  1. Find the number of uses for which the plans cost the same.

    [2]

  2. Give the cost of either plan at that number of uses.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Set the expressions equal. Subtract \(5x\) from both sides to leave \(18=2x+4\).

Subtract 4 from both sides and divide by 2.

\(7\)

(b) Put 7 in place of x in either plan.

\(53\)

examples.title: Equation containing a fraction
examples.question:
A mystery number t is shared into 3 equal amounts. After giving away 2, one share has 7 left.

  1. Find t.

    [2]

  2. Write the original equation and check the solution.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The equation is \(\frac{t}{3}-2=7\). Add 2 to both sides.

Multiply both sides by 3 to find the original amount.

\(27\)

(b) For t = 27, one share is 9. Removing 2 leaves 7.

\(\frac{t}{3}-2=7\)

examples.title: Using a formula in reverse
examples.question:
A score is given by \(P=5t-7\), with t the number of sessions.

  1. The score is 3. Find the session count.

    [2]

  2. Rearrange the formula to make t the subject.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Use \(3=5t-7\). Add 7, then divide by 5.

\(2\)

(b) Add 7 to both sides, then divide both sides by 5. The left side is now t.

\(t=\frac{P+7}{5}\)

examples.title: Choosing a whole-number value within two bounds
examples.question:
A club rule requires a whole-number age a. It says \(17\lt a\le 23\).

  1. Write the largest allowed age.

    [2]

  2. Draw a number line for this interval and explain whether the lower endpoint is included.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The right-hand end is \(23\).

The sign includes equality, so the end value is allowed.

\(23\)

(b) A strict inequality gives an open circle. A sign with equality gives a filled circle.

Open circle at 17, filled circle at 23, and a line joining them.
